proof:
# Power moment ratios of a concave sequence

## 1. The finite inequality

Let `f_0,...,f_(N-1)` be a nonnegative, nonzero concave sequence, with
`N>=1`, and let `m=max_i f_i>0`. For every REAL `p>=1`,

    (p+2) sum_i f_i^(p+1) -(p+1)m sum_i f_i^p
                       >= m^(p+1)/N.                  (1)

In particular,

    sum_i f_i^(p+1) > [(p+1)/(p+2)]m sum_i f_i^p.      (2)

The coefficient `(p+1)/(p+2)` is sharp uniformly over finite lengths.
The finite correction in (1) is not asserted sharp for each p and N.
All powers in the statement have positive exponent, so zero terms cause
no ambiguity. The proof uses only a quadratic inequality and integration
of positive level truncations; it does not transfer continuous Berwald
inequalities to integer samples.

## 2. A self-contained quadratic starting point

For an integer `h>=0`, among all concave REAL sequences `x_0,...,x_h`
with `x_0=1`, the quadratic

    sum_i [x_i^2-(2/3)x_i]

has minimum `(h+1)/[3(2h+1)]`, attained by
`v_i=1-2i/(2h+1)`.

Here are the finite details. The case h=0 is direct. For h>=1 write
`e_i=x_i-v_i`, so e is concave and e_0=0. The exact Green representation is

    e_i=(i/h)e_h+sum_(t=1)^(h-1) a_t G_t(i),
    a_t=2e_t-e_(t-1)-e_(t+1)>=0,
    G_t(i)=min(i,t)-it/h.

Both sides have equal second differences and equal endpoint values, which
proves the representation. Put `r_i=v_i-1/3`. Direct sums of the affine
pieces give

    sum_i i r_i=0,
    sum_i r_i G_t(i)=t(h-t)(h+1-t)/[3(2h+1)]>=0.

Consequently `sum r_i e_i>=0`, and expansion gives

    sum[x_i^2-(2/3)x_i]-sum[v_i^2-(2/3)v_i]
                 =sum e_i^2+2sum r_i e_i>=0.

The displayed value at v follows by summing integers and squares.

Now let `g_0,...,g_(n-1)` be nonnegative and concave, with maximum b>0
at index j. Normalize by b and apply the preceding one-sided statement
to each side of j, with the left side reversed. Subtract the double-counted
peak term `1/3`. This yields

    sum g_i^2 -(2/3)b sum g_i
      >=(b^2/6)[1/(2j+1)+1/(2(n-1-j)+1)]
      >=b^2/(3n).                                    (3)

The last inequality is `1/A+1/B>=4/(A+B)` with `A+B=2n`.
Thus (1) holds already at p=1. This is also valid for n=1.

## 3. Level integration proves every real p>1

By homogeneity take m=1. For `0<=t<1` define

    g_i(t)=(f_i-t)_+.

Its positive indices form one consecutive block. On that block it is a
positive concave sequence, with maximum `1-t`, and the block has at most
N terms. Applying (3) there and adjoining the zero terms only in sums gives

    sum_i g_i(t)^2 -(2/3)(1-t)sum_i g_i(t)
                              >=(1-t)^2/(3N).         (4)

This step does NOT claim that adjoining zero terms preserves concavity.
The quadratic inequality was applied only on the actual positive block.

Fix p>1, multiply (4) by `t^(p-2)`, and integrate on `[0,1]`.
All integrands are bounded apart from the integrable endpoint factor
`t^(p-2)`, and there are finitely many terms. For `0<=f<=1`, elementary
integration gives

    integral_0^f t^(p-2)(f-t)^2 dt
       =2f^(p+1)/[(p-1)p(p+1)],

    integral_0^f t^(p-2)(1-t)(f-t) dt
       =f^p/[p(p-1)]-f^(p+1)/[p(p+1)],

    integral_0^1 t^(p-2)(1-t)^2 dt
       =2/[(p-1)p(p+1)].                              (5)

Writing `A=sum f_i^(p+1)` and `B=sum f_i^p`, the integrated left side of
(4) is

    2[(p+2)A-(p+1)B]/[3(p-1)p(p+1)].

The integrated right side is the same positive prefactor divided by N.
Cancelling proves `(p+2)A-(p+1)B>=1/N`. Rescaling proves (1), and the
strict homogeneous inequality (2) follows from its positive correction.

## 4. Sharpness of the homogeneous coefficient

For fixed p>=1 take the triangular sequence

    f_i=1-|i|/h,  -h<=i<=h,  h>=1.

Its maximum is one. The Riemann sums for the two continuous powers give

    (1/h)sum_i f_i^p ->2/(p+1),
    (1/h)sum_i f_i^(p+1) ->2/(p+2).

Therefore the ratio in (2) approaches `(p+1)/(p+2)`. A one-sided arithmetic
sequence gives the same limit. The theorem itself and its positive finite
correction hold for every finite sequence; only sharpness uses a limit.

## 5. The value at an integer mean under powered weights

Let d>=1 be real, put `w_i=f_i^d`, and assume its weighted mean

    j=(sum_i i w_i)/(sum_i w_i)

is an integer. Concavity of the piecewise linear interpolation of f and
Jensen's inequality imply

    f_j >= [sum_i f_i^(d+1)]/[sum_i f_i^d].

Consequently, if `W=sum_i w_i` and `w_max=m^d`, then

    f_j >= [(d+1)/(d+2)]m
                    +m^(d+1)/[(d+2)NW],              (6)

and in particular

    w_j > [(d+1)/(d+2)]^d w_max.                      (7)

The integer mean is inside the index interval; the positive right side in
(6) also proves that its fiber weight is positive. Neither the concavity of
w itself nor a replacement of the integer sum by an integral is assumed.

The coefficient in (7) is sharp even with EXACTLY integer means. To show
this, use `f_i(L)=(L-i)_+` at nonnegative integer indices and weights
`f_i(L)^d`. Their mean `m_d(L)` is continuous for `L>1`, including integer
values of L because a newly born term has zero weight. It is strictly
increasing: on any fixed positive support interval and for j>i, the ratio
`[(L-j)/(L-i)]^d` strictly increases with L. Expanding the difference of
weighted means as a finite sum over ordered pairs gives strict increase
whenever at least two positive terms occur; new support points strengthen
it. Moreover `m_d(L)->0` as `L` decreases to1, while Riemann sums give

    m_d(L)/L ->1/(d+2)  as L->infinity.

Thus for every integer k>=1 there exists L_k>1 with `m_d(L_k)=k`, and
necessarily `L_k->infinity`. At this integer mean,

    w_k/w_max=((L_k-k)/L_k)^d
                    ->[(d+1)/(d+2)]^d.

For integer d, these are actual mixed-volume profiles of the convex cone
`{(z,x):0<=z<=L_k, x in (L_k-z)K}`, where K is any d-dimensional convex
body. The possible apex fiber has zero d-volume and does not affect the
mean. Hence the sharpness statement is also realizable by actual convex
fibers, not merely by abstract weighted sequences.

## 6. Geometric scope

For one integer coordinate, Brunn–Minkowski makes the dth roots of positive
d-dimensional convex fiber volumes a concave sequence. Equations (6),(7)
therefore give a lower bound on the volume of the fiber at the TRUE
integer-valued mixed centroid in every continuous dimension. They do not
by themselves bound an oblique cap's mass or guarantee that the mixed
centroid has integer base. No global OC conclusion is drawn.
